description: AllO2 is a team made up of medical engineering, automation and technological physics students. Our main goal is to provide a feasible way for astronauts to monitor their health status while exploration missions are in progress.
summary:
COGNIS is an assessment tool based on the GRIP system implemented by the ESA. Using a three-part testing system, the medical team in charge of the crew can monitor variations in musculoskeletal integrity, visual disturbances caused by the fluid shift phenomenon in microgravity, and neurobehavioral patterns. Our integrated system stores daily assessments and sends them to Earth through our application once per week for a full analysis. 
COGNIS combines existing musculoskeletal testing with two new diagnostic tools: a three-part visual acuity exam (featuring a Tumbling Arrow, an Amsler grid, and a Sloan letter contrast test) and vocal biomarker analysis that tracks jitter and shimmer against a pre-mission baseline. Together, these capabilities position COGNIS as the future of multi-system health monitoring.
details:
COGNIS is a compact, handheld daily assessment station that gives a medical team a continuous, quantitative picture of three body systems known to change during long-duration space missions: the musculoskeletal system, vision, and neurobehavioral state. Each daily session takes about 10-15 minutes and has three modules:

  1. Grip assessment (musculoskeletal and sensorimotor). Inspired by the instrumented manipulandum used in ESA’s GRIP experiment on the ISS, COGNIS uses a spring-resisted ring around a central sensor pole. The astronaut twists the central pole in pronation and supination, and the device records peak grip strength, force over time, and how steadily force is held. COGNIS’s grip data adds a daily, functional view of musculoskeletal deconditioning alongside those measures. 
    • Tumbling Arrow acuity test for near visual acuity, where SANS-related shifts in focus often show up first
    • Amsler grid to detect distortion or blind spots in central vision
    • Sloan letter contrast sensitivity test, which can reveal subtle declines in visual function before acuity changes
  2. Vocal biomarker analysis (neurobehavioral monitoring). The astronaut records a short standardized set of phrases (connected speech) and a sustained vowel. COGNIS extracts acoustic features, mainly jitter (cycle-to-cycle variation in pitch) and shimmer (cycle-to-cycle variation in loudness). These are compared against the individual’s own baseline to track signs of fatigue, stress, and changes in cognitive or emotional state over the mission.

Data flow. Every session is timestamped and stored on board. A local analysis layer compares each result against the astronaut’s personal baseline and flags anything outside a set threshold, and those flags are queued for immediate downlink. The complete dataset is bundled and sent to the ground team once a week for full trend analysis, so routine data uses little bandwidth while clinically relevant changes reach the ground right away.

Personal baselines. Every measurement is compared to the astronaut’s own baseline, not to population norms. Baselines are recorded before the mission and then re-established in flight after the initial adaptation period, because fluid shift may cause edema, which in turn leads to abnormalities in speech patterns. This separates real decline from the expected effects of being in microgravity.

Benefits

  • Daily, not occasional: Most in-flight medical assessments happen at fixed points in the mission. COGNIS adds a daily trend line between them, so gradual changes are caught earlier.
  • Three systems, one short session: One device and one routine replace three separate checks, which saves crew time, one of the scarcest resources on a mission.
  • Non-invasive and self-administered: No needles, no electrodes, and no second crew member needed.
  • Low bandwidth: Only a weekly data bundle plus urgent flags, which suits missions where communication with Earth is limited or delayed.
  • Personalized: Comparing each astronaut to their own baseline cuts false alarms caused by normal differences between people.

Intended impact
COGNIS is built for missions beyond low Earth orbit, such as Artemis, lunar surface stays, and eventually Mars, where communication delays and the lack of immediate evacuation mean crews need more autonomous health monitoring. Catching declines in grip strength, vision, or mental state early gives flight surgeons time to adjust exercise, workload, sleep, or countermeasures before a problem affects safety or performance. The same approach could be repurposed on Earth for remote or isolated populations, such as Antarctic stations, submarine crews, rural telemedicine, or older patients monitored at home.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

  • Hardware: ATI Nano25 Transducer, Arduino Uno, Al6061-T6 housing, mechanism and chin rest designed and validated in SolidWorks.
  • Software: Python, MySQL, Praat / Parselmouth, application. 
  • Data and references: Pelli-Robson, CAPE-V clinical voice protocol, https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/hazard-gravity-fields/; https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20220008786; https://www.nasa.gov/reference/about-human-factors-and-behavioral-performance/; https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/esdmd/hhp/behavioral-health-risk/; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21849212/; https://zenodo.org/records/14259374; https://physionet.org/content/b2ai-voice/4.0.0/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8138221/; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21849212/; https://www.mdpi.com/2075-1729/4/4/621

How it’s creative
COGNIS takes an instrument concept already utilized aboard the ISS and transforms it into a daily clinical tool. It brings together three tests (strength testing, eye testing, and voice analysis) normally done with separate equipment in separate settings, since as per our research, visual acuity is not currently performed in-mission, into one portable device and one short routine. The voice module stands out: it monitors mental and cognitive state using nothing more than a microphone and a 30-second recording, with no questionnaires and no extra sensors. By re-baselining in flight, COGNIS also treats the microgravity environment as a variable to measure, not just noise in the data.

Factors our team considered

  • Crew time: Each daily session is short and doesn’t need a second person.
  • Mass, volume, and power: The device is compact, which matters on any spacecraft.
  • Microgravity use: A fixed chin rest keeps the viewing distance at 40 cm, and the grip design can be fixed to a surface using U-clips.
  • Confounding factors: Cabin noise, fluid-shift effects on the voice, time of day, and the astronaut’s place in their sleep cycle can all skew results. Sessions are scheduled at a consistent time, and baselines are re-established in flight.
  • False alarms vs. missed findings: Alert thresholds are set to minimize unnecessary alarms that would erode crew trust in the system, while still catching real changes.
  • Privacy and medical data security: Data is encrypted on board and in transit, ensuring only the medical team can access it.
  • Scope and honesty: COGNIS is a screening and trend-tracking tool. It complements onboard diagnostic imaging such as OCT and formal medical exams rather than replacing them.
  • Interdisciplinary design: Our team of five combines medical engineering, automation and computer science, and theoretical physics, so clinical, hardware, software, and signal-processing decisions were made together.
